strings: Conventional (non-neuroengineering) alignment research and oversight methods; S28 coded as comparator source.
Labour-replacing AI without the neurotech family (S15 definition; Drago & Laine 2025).
Other (specify) '- used for the representational-constraint proposal (S01)

Three independent book-length arguments (S20, S21, S22) predict displacement of biological workers and wage pressure on emulations. None proposes a mechanism that preserves biological humans' bargaining power, and the ownership gate is not passed.

The only agency-strengthening evidence is therapeutic and individual, not bargaining power. The enhancement pathway has no specified mechanism, access model or ownership terms (S11, S14), while workplace and state pathways weaken agency (S19, S29).

Whole brain emulation: scanning a specific human brain at sufficient resolution and running a computational model that reproduces that person's cognition (stages S1 component simulation → S6 deployed populations). Systems that model only parts of a brain are not treated as WBE (e.g., partial emulation and digital twins (S1-S2)).
WBE-O AI overseer · WBE-R alignment researcher · WBE-G general-purpose AI system · WBE-L digital labour · WBE-I institutional decision-making (provisional)

Claimed beneficiaries: humanity at large via aligned intelligence (WBE-O/R/G); owners of scans, emulations and compute (WBE-L). Bear risks: emulated persons (copying, deletion, subsistence); biological workers (displacement); scanned originals (consent); everyone (capability spillover).
Long (> 15 y). No source dates S3; S13: whole-brain simulation 'many years out'; S21: de novo AI plausibly first.
Alignment: conventional (non-neuro) alignment and oversight methods (S28). IC: labour-replacing AI without WBE (D05).
Alignment: value specification (WBE-G), scalable oversight (WBE-O), research acceleration (WBE-R). Intelligence Curse: claimed by no source as a benefit; displacement argued (S20-S22). → Both

Brain-computer interfaces: devices that record (read) and/or stimulate (write) neural activity and couple it to computers or AI systems; invasive and non-invasive; stages S1 passive decoding → S4 population-scale deployment.

BCI-D neural data for alignment · BCI-O bandwidth for oversight · BCI-E enhancement / merger · BCI-T therapeutic · BCI-W workplace · BCI-P consumer · BCI-S state/security · BCI-X representational constraint

Claimed beneficiaries: AI developers (better feedback signals); overseers; impaired persons (BCI-T); enhanced users. Bear risks: users (manipulation, mental privacy, neuroplasticity); workers (surveillance); citizens and detainees (state monitoring); non-users (inequality).

Near for BCI-T, BCI-W, BCI-P (devices in trials or on market: FDA IDE registrations, S16 E075; workplace EEG, S19). Medium-Long for BCI-D/O/E (only toy-task or argued evidence: S24-S27, S14). S09 claims a 5-year horizon (not accessed; tier D).
Alignment: RLHF / RLAIF and non-BCI oversight tooling (S28). IC: labour-replacing AI without BCI (D05).

Alignment: value specification / preference elicitation (BCI-D), oversight (BCI-O), research acceleration (BCI-E). IC: enhancement keeps humans relevant (BCI-E, argued); disempowerment pathways (BCI-W/S/P). → Both

Brain-inspired computing: neuromorphic hardware (spiking, in-memory, self-assembled substrates), brain-inspired AGI architectures with human-like motivational systems, and models constrained by neural data. Family boundary open (D03).
NM-H hardware / efficient compute · NM-A brain-inspired AGI architecture · NM-N neural-data-constrained models · NM-E edge / decentralised deployment
Near for NM-H (chips exist: S05, S07). Long for NM-A (S30 argued only). NM-N: projected compute far beyond GPT-4 for human-level robustness (S13).
Alignment: non-neuromorphic AI and standard robustness / interpretability methods (adversarial training: S13). IC: concentrated cloud AI (D05).

Alignment: interpretability/robustness (NM-N), value specification via motivational architecture (NM-A), verification (NM-H). IC: no source claims a benefit (NM-E decentralisation unclaimed). → Alignment

Five prerequisites: (P1) whole-brain scanning of a human brain; (P2) models turning structure into dynamics; (P3) compute and storage to run in real time; (P4) a validation method; (P5) body and environment input/output. Met = all five at the scale the use needs. Partly = at least one at mammalian whole-brain scale.
E037, E043, E065 (components demonstrated; whole brain argued)
P2 turning a connectome into a runnable model; P1 scanning throughput
No date in any source; signals point to a long horizon (S13 'many years out'; S21 expects other AI first)
Best result: 1 mm³ of human cortex (S16), about a millionth of the brain. Evidence on parts of the brain does not meet the whole-emulation criterion.
Met now at laboratory scale (S24, S26)
Decoding replicated in lab tasks (S26, S27); closed-loop training only in simple tasks (S24, S25). Clinical implants (S16) are therapy evidence, not alignment evidence.
S09 likely relevant but not accessible.

No method to validate reproduced properties (S17); no theory of simulation stability (S13)
Decoding accuracy: F1 67% for two classes, 46% for three (S27); missed errors harm learning (S26)
E077 (small-task demonstration for neural-data models; argued for AGI)
No framework to confirm fidelity (S17); neural-data gains are narrow (S13)
Fidelity (M2) holds for the subjective runtime the use needs and survives copying.
Chaotic long-run dynamics; gap between simulation and reality (S13)
Decoding meets M2 across sessions, people and at least 2 task types without full recalibration.
Variation between people; about 200 calibration trials; losses across tasks (S26); partly reduced by pre-training across people (S27)
M5 Scalable manufacture, compute and data
Recording 10⁴ neurons by 2035 (S13) is far below whole-brain needs; the low-fidelity route needs about 10⁶ hours of data (S16)
Recording capacity projected to 2035 (S13); whole-brain scale not dated

About 73 times more tokens per second per watt (NorthPole vs H100) and about 1,000 times lower energy per small-image inference (Loihi 2), as reported by S05. Efficiency is not cost: no total cost-of-ownership model.
E075, E084, E114 (demonstrated for clinical use; argued otherwise)

Inherited values would include aggression, power-seeking and other human failings (E039). Not answered.
Values drift under acceleration, copying, selection and long subjective runtime (E062, E091, E090). Not answered.
Competing approach: other advanced AI and conventional alignment are likely to arrive first, so the window may not exist (E038, E092, E007). Answered only by argument (S16).
WBE research speeds up unaligned AI more than aligned intelligence (E040, E068). Answered only by argument (S16).
Cheap copyable labour removes workers' bargaining power; only asset holders benefit, if property rights hold (E087, E089, E095). Not answered.
Decoding is too inaccurate and person-specific; missed errors harm learning more than false alarms (E103, E106). Partly answered: pre-training across people (E107).
Alternative explanation: gains may come from more feedback, not new information; no study compares an equal amount of explicit feedback (E099, E101, E108). Not stated by any source; not answered.
Competing approach: resources would do more good on interpretability; the limits of feedback-based training apply to neural feedback too (E056, E109). Not answered.
BCIs give only a fixed speed-up; a scaled AI outpaces it (E049, E051). Not answered.
The interface becomes an attack channel: an AI could hijack the user or manipulate what an overseer sees (E052, E053). Answered only by argument: read-only interfaces (S14).
Enhancement helps capability researchers equally, and an unaligned AI would want to remove merged humans (E050, E055). Not answered.
Counter-view: anti-coercion and mental-privacy safeguards could limit the harm. Proposals only (S29).
Theories of brain computation are underdetermined by data, so fidelity cannot be confirmed (E117, E077). Not answered.
Social drives may be unstable: self-reward hacking, self-modification or antisocial development, raised by the proponent source itself (E121). Answered only by argument: designed upbringing (E120).
Full behavioural verification is out of reach for any sufficiently complex AGI (E118). Not answered.
Alternative explanation: gains may come from general regularisation, not brain-likeness; the gain vanished with noise (E045). Not answered.
Competing approach: adversarial training beats neural-data augmentation for robustness, 68% vs 62% (E045). Not answered.
On-chip learning defeats weight-inspection audits; no hardware-level interpretability research exists (E012, E013, E021). Answered only by argument: weight-change monitoring, untested (E017).
Small fabrication runs raise costs, and no source claims edge deployment spreads power (E016).

Relocates the problem: value specification becomes the fidelity and stability of emulated humans; oversight becomes aligning the overseer (S13, S16, S21). Creates new agents whose alignment, welfare and governance are open (S16, S21, S22).

Value inheritance and human-derived oversight are argued by S16 and partly S14, but S13 judges the WBE-safety arguments flawed and S13 and S21 expect other AI first. Technical capability is shown only for 1 mm³ of cortex (S16), and value drift is raised by S16 and S21. Every pathway has a contrary or conflicting necessary link and otherwise rests on argument or assumption. Low confidence: no source tests any alignment link.
No entry addresses supervising a more capable system (WBE-O-L4) or compares with non-WBE oversight (WBE-O-L5).
Only an assumed claim that depends on fidelity (S16); no comparison with AI research agents.
Value inheritance argued (S16) and disputed (S13); drift raised (S16, S21); timing contrary (S13, S21).

Partly relocates the problem: adds a feedback channel but inherits the limits of feedback-based training (S28) and adds manipulation risk (S14). No new agents, but a new attack surface on humans (S14, S16).

Prerequisites are shown at laboratory scale: single-trial error signals (S26), EEG-rewarded learning on robotic tasks (S25), fNIRS classification at F1 46-67% (S27). The decisive links (information gain, resistance to gaming, transfer to frontier models) have no evidence either way, and S14 argues the oversight gain is a fixed speed-up. Neither the Moderate nor the Weak condition is met.
Decoding and small-task training shown; no test of information gain over explicit feedback (BCI-D-L3) or of transfer to frontier models (BCI-D-L6).
Fixed speed-up argument (S14) unanswered; security contrary (S14, S16).
Relocates the problem: replaces objective specification with design of a motivational architecture (S30). May create new agents if brain-inspired agents have moral status; no source addresses it.

S30 (peer-reviewed, affiliated authors) argues brain-like motivational systems make human-style safety reasoning appropriate, but also lists instability risks and notes the theories are underdetermined. The only empirical result (S13) is a small-benchmark gain smaller than a non-neural method. Hardware sources concern governance, not alignment benefit (S05-S07).
All support argued by affiliated authors (S30); stability contrary (S30).
S30 argues verification of any AGI is intractable, which moves the problem rather than showing an advantage.
Own experiments: adversarial training stronger; gain vanished with noise (S13).
Agnostic. S22 assumes suitably designed digital minds could be conscious but commits to no theory; S16 notes uncertainty only during testing.
Psychological capacities and potentials, not a single property (S22)

Deepens replacement: emulation labour substitutes for biological labour (S20, S21); digital populations may dilute transfers and political power (S22).

Not specified: fabrication, models, deployment control and efficiency gains unaddressed (S05 notes small fabrication runs only).

Who owns the scans? No (S16 does not cover ownership). Who owns the emulations? Partly: emulations act as economic agents, human asset ownership assumed (S20, unverified). Can emulations own assets? No.
Transfers diluted toward digital subsistence (S22); returns to asset holders only (S20).
Who receives returns from emulation labour? Partly: asset holders (S20, unverified); transfers diluted (S22).
Rapidly copying digital minds could gain majority control (S22); concentration of power listed (S16). Influence through emulations is not biological-human influence.
Can users refuse without exclusion (work, insurance, services)? Partly: limited freedom to refuse (S19); consent alone is inadequate (S29).
Enhancement could keep humans competitive (S11, assumed) but may deepen inequality (S11) and still lose to AI-only systems (S14).
State neural monitoring to detect dissent (S29).
Clinical BCIs restore communication and movement (S03, S16). Individual agency, not bargaining power.
Who owns and may use neural data? No (S29 explicitly leaves it open; legal classification unclear).
No source claims an effect; S05 does not analyse power.
Who owns fabrication capacity? No (S05 notes small fabrication runs only). Who owns the models? No.
Edge efficiency shown (S05), but its effect on control is not analysed; efficiency is a prerequisite, not evidence about control.

Asset ownership (S20, unverified); basic income (S22 says fiscal capacity may run out)

Suffering across copies; copying, modification or deletion without consent; subsistence and selection; labour displacement; political dominance of digital minds; value drift; information hazards (R01-R06, R20, R21)

Severity follows from unbounded copy numbers and subjective speed (S22). No source estimates likelihood. Harms are hard to detect and hard to reverse once copies exist; proposed safeguards are principles only (S22).
Manipulation through the interface; workplace neurosurveillance; state monitoring; commercial exploitation; neural-data theft; neuroplastic change; bias; inequality (R07-R14)

Two independent sources (S19 peer-reviewed; S29 policy paper) identify the workplace mechanism; others are argued. Employers, states and vendors hold control; consent is judged inadequate (S29). Likelihood is not assessable from the database.

Hardware attacks; unauditable on-device learning; escape from compute-threshold rules and export controls; opaque self-assembled hardware; unstable AGI values; unrecognised moral status (R15-R19, R22)

Governance risks are argued by preprints (S05-S07) and one peer-reviewed argument (S30). On-chip learning defeats weight inspection and countermeasures are immature. Only one risk has a likelihood judgment (S06: low for current devices).
